articles.title: Spokane wildfires: Map, smoke tracking tools, and latest update as 3 fires devastate eastern Washington
articles.description: A series of devastating wildfires near Spokane, Washington, has destroyed roughly 600 structures, forced the evacuation of thousands of people, and remained 0% contained as of Monday morning. The fires—collectively being referred to as the Spokane Complex Fire—have so far burned more than 7,700 acres, NBC News reports . The Complex Fire comprises three distinct fires: the Old Trails Fire, the Fairview Fire, and the Autumn Lane Fire. Spokane is Washington’s second largest city and located in the eastern part of the state, near the boarder with Idaho. Lisa Brown, the city’s mayor, said in a news conference on Sunday that the fires are “the worst natural disaster our region has faced.” As of early Monday, almost 900 firefighters and other personnel were working contain the fires , USA Today reports. The cause, yet to be determined, is still under investigation. So far, no injuries have been reported. How to track the Spokane, Washington, fires If you’re looking to track the fires, stay on top of the latest alerts, or follow the latest smoke and air-quality data, we’ve rounded up some resources below. WFCA.com : The mapping tool from the Western Fire Chiefs lets you pull up various details of any fire. Using data from NASA and NOAA, the tool provides a real-time snapshot and gives you details like a current “threat score” for each fire. Find it here . Watch Duty : This app and mapping tool from the nonprofit Watch Duty offers up-to-date information about evacuation orders, details about local shelters, and information about local firefighter personnel. Find it here . Wildfire Aware : This app, powered by spatial analytics company Esri, let’s you search any active fire in the United States and track its location and spread at a very granular level. articles.title: Nigeria Food Security Outlook Update, June 2026 - January 2027: Escalating North West conflict drives higher needs amid protracted North East insecurity
articles.description: Country: Nigeria Source: Famine Early Warning System Network Please refer to the attached file. Key Messages Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes persist in inaccessible areas of the North East — including Abadam, Bama, Guzamala, and Marte local government areas (LGAs) — where severe movement restrictions cut households off from farmland, markets, and assistance, driving large, persistent food consumption gaps. These outcomes are expected to continue through January 2027, as access constraints will prevent affected populations from benefiting from the October–December main harvest Escalating conflict across northern Nigeria is disrupting livelihoods and driving displacement, sustaining Crisis (IPC Phase 3) outcomes among conflict-affected and displaced populations. Conflict has risen sharply in the North West and North Central, where restricted farmland access — including armed group control over harvested crops — will limit seasonal improvement through the projection period. Poor macroeconomic conditions continue to erode household purchasing power despite headline improvements. Despite improvements in oil production, GDP growth, external reserves, and exchange rate stability, inflation remains high. Rising food, transport, and energy costs, coupled with staple food prices — rice, maize, millet, and sorghum — remaining above the five-year average amid below-average market supply and heavy market dependence, continue to pressure households. The October-December harvest is expected to drive uneven improvement. Households with access to land and assets will improve to Stressed (IPC Phase 2) or Minimal (IPC Phase 1), while poorer households, IDPs, and those in the worst conflict-affected areas will remain in Crisis (IPC Phase 3) through January 2027. FEWS NET estimates 21-22 million people will remain in need of humanitarian food assistance through January 2027, with needs peaking during the June-August lean season as food stocks deplete and staple prices reach seasonal highs. Despite seasonal improvement from the main harvest, the scale of need will remain at a historic high, as conflict- and macroeconomicdriven losses of income and production will prevent millions of poor and displaced households from meeting their basic food needs.
